turns.doctor_question: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. To get us started, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Dr. Smith, I... I guess I'm here because things have been getting a bit complicated at work lately. I've been a retail supervisor for years, you know, managing the floor, handling the team, making sure everything runs smoothly. But recently, when I try to sit down and explain the inventory numbers for the week, or... or even just go over the weekend schedule with the staff, it's like my brain just takes off in a dozen different directions at once. 

I'll start talking about the stock levels, and then suddenly I'm talking about the delivery trucks, which reminds me that Thursday is usually a heavy delivery day, but Thursday is also when we have the church grill out back, and then I start thinking about the way my boss sounded when he asked me about the grill last week—his tone was just... off, you know? And before I know it, I'm trying to explain all of this at the same time, and the words are just jumping from the trucks to Thursdays to the church grill to my boss's tone, and I look up and... well, my team is just staring at me. They have these blank looks on their faces, like they can't follow a single word I'm saying. It's frustrating because it all makes perfect sense in my head, but when it comes out, it's like a tangled ball of yarn and they just... they don't get it. And it's really starting to become a problem on the floor, you know?

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient describes their speech jumping between loosely connected topics (trucks, Thursdays, church grill, boss's tone) to the point where others cannot follow what they are saying.
symptom_reasoning.S038: The patient describes the subjective experience of their brain taking off 'in a dozen different directions at once,' indicating racing thoughts or flight of ideas.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: Aside from the trouble staying focused at work, have you been feeling unusually energetic, or like you need much less sleep than normal lately?
turns.patient_response:
Energetic? Oh, no, no. Definitely not energetic. If anything, Dr. Smith, it's quite the opposite when it comes to my physical energy. You see, being on the retail floor all day at my age—I'm 59 now—it really takes a toll on the joints. I'm on my feet from the moment I clock in. Well, technically I get there about fifteen minutes early, around 7:15 AM, just to walk the perimeter and check the endcaps before the doors open, but by the time I get home at night, I am absolutely wiped out. I have this brown leather recliner in my living room, great lumbar support, and the second I sit down in it, I just deflate like an old tire. 

So there's certainly no unusual burst of energy going on. And as for sleep... well, I definitely still need my sleep. I try my hardest to get my full eight hours every single night. Sometimes it's hard to drift off right away because my mind is doing that... that tangled yarn thing I was just telling you about, spinning around the inventory and the schedules and my boss, but I really *want* to sleep. I crave it. I certainly don't feel like I can just skip it or run on fumes. 

If I get anything less than seven hours, I'm dragging my feet the whole next day. Like last Tuesday, the neighbor's golden retriever was barking at all hours—nice dog usually, but he just wouldn't quit at the fence—and I only got maybe five hours of rest. I was utterly exhausted by noon on Wednesday, just drinking coffee after coffee in the breakroom. So, no, I haven't noticed needing less sleep at all, or feeling super energized. I just feel like a regular, tired guy who can't get his words straight when he needs to.

symptom_reasoning.S027: The patient mentions that sometimes it is hard to drift off to sleep right away because his mind is spinning about work.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient explicitly denies feeling unusually energetic, stating he is 'absolutely wiped out' after a day of work.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient explicitly denies needing less sleep, emphasizing that he craves his full eight hours and feels exhausted if he gets less.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any problems with your memory, such as forgetting where you put things, losing track of appointments, or having trouble finding the right words for common objects?
turns.patient_response:
Memory? No, no, my memory is... well, it's sharp as a tack, honestly. I haven't been losing things or missing appointments. In fact, just the other day, I was looking for my favorite pen—it's this blue Pilot G2, 0.7 millimeter, the only kind I like to use for signing off on the delivery manifests because the ink flows so nicely and doesn't smudge on that cheap carbon paper they use. Anyway, I thought I'd lost it, but I closed my eyes and retraced my steps perfectly. I remembered exactly where I'd set it down: right next to the cash register on register three, right after I helped ring out a customer who was buying three packs of those AA batteries that we had on sale on the endcap. 

And appointments, I never miss those. I have my dentist appointment next Thursday at 3:15 PM, Dr. Henderson over on Maple Street, and I've had that written in my planner for six months. I even know that my car registration is due on the 14th of next month. So, no, keeping track of things isn't the issue at all. 

And as for finding words for things... no, I know exactly what everything is called. I know a stapler is a stapler, a pallet jack is a pallet jack. The words themselves are all there, sitting right in my head, clear as day. It's just... it's just what happens when I try to string them all together into a sentence that makes sense to somebody else. The words are fine, the memory is fine. It's the... the traffic control in my head, I guess you could call it. That's what's broken. But remembering where I put my keys or my glasses? No, I've got a system for that. Keys go in the ceramic bowl by the front door—the one my sister got me from her trip to Santa Fe back in 2018—the very second I walk in the house. Never lose 'em.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient explicitly describes an inability to string words together into coherent sentences ('traffic control in my head... is broken') and exhibits highly detailed, circumstantial speech.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly denies losing things, stating they have a system for their keys and 'never lose 'em.'
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient explicitly denies missing appointments, noting they keep track of them perfectly in a planner.
symptom_reasoning.S031: The patient explicitly denies having memory problems or word-finding difficulties, stating their memory is 'sharp as a tack.'

turns.doctor_question: Have you had any recent physical health problems, head injuries, or new medications that started around the same time this difficulty with your thoughts began?
turns.patient_response:
Physical health problems or head injuries? No, no, nothing like that. I haven't hit my head or been in any accidents. The last time I had any kind of real physical issue was... oh, gosh, it must have been three years ago when I pulled a muscle in my lower back trying to lift a display case that was way too heavy for one person. But that healed up just fine after a few weeks of physical therapy and some muscle relaxers they gave me at the time. 

And as for new medications, no, nothing new there either. I've been taking the same blood pressure medication—Lisinopril, 10 milligrams, a little pink pill—every morning with my breakfast for the last five years. My doctor, Dr. Evans, he's a great guy, always says my pressure is right where it needs to be, usually around 120 over 80, give or take a point or two depending on if I've had my morning coffee yet. I take a multivitamin, too, just a generic one from the pharmacy down the street, the one with extra vitamin D because I don't get out in the sun much working retail all day. 

But no new pills, no changes to my diet, no falls, no bumps on the head. I haven't even had a cold lately. I'm generally pretty healthy for a guy pushing sixty, you know? I try to eat right, mostly chicken and vegetables, maybe a steak once a month as a treat. So, no, there's no obvious physical reason why my thoughts are suddenly getting all tangled up like this. It just sort of... started happening on its own, without any warning or any changes in my routine. I wish it was as simple as a new medication causing a side effect, because then I could just stop taking it and go back to normal, but unfortunately, that's just not the case. It's just my brain doing this... this weird thing all by itself.

turns.doctor_question: When your mind is racing and you're trying to explain things to your team, do you find yourself feeling a sense of overwhelming worry, dread, or apprehension about the future or about things going wrong?
turns.patient_response:
Worry? Dread? Oh, no, no, it's not like I'm having a panic attack or anything like that. I don't feel like the sky is falling or that the store is going to burn down. It's not a fearful feeling at all, really. I mean, sure, I want things to go right because I take pride in my work—I've been managing teams for over fifteen years, and I like a tight ship. I like when the floor is faced properly, when the tags are all facing forward, and the aisles are clear of pallets before we open the doors at 8:00 AM. 

But when I'm standing there with the morning crew—usually it's Dave from electronics, Sarah from apparel, and maybe one or two of the new part-timers—and I'm trying to give them the game plan for the day... I don't feel scared or worried about the future. I'm not dreading what's going to happen. It's just... I know exactly what needs to be done. I see the whole plan in my head. I see the truck manifest, I know we have three pallets of seasonal goods that need to be broken down, I know the registers need till audits... but when I open my mouth to tell them, the words just bottleneck. 

It's frustrating, certainly. Extremely frustrating. It makes me feel embarrassed, like I look foolish in front of my own staff, you know? But it's not dread. I'm not standing there thinking something terrible is about to happen to me or to them. I'm just standing there thinking, "Come on, Frank, just say the sentence. Just tell Dave to take the pallet jack to aisle four." But instead, it comes out all jumbled, like I'm trying to talk around a mouthful of marbles. So, no, it's not an overwhelming worry or apprehension about the future. It's just an overwhelming frustration with my own mouth in that exact moment.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient describes their speech as coming out 'all jumbled' and words bottlenecking when trying to communicate.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient explicitly denies feeling worry, dread, or apprehension about the future.

turns.doctor_question: Does this same feeling of your words becoming a 'tangled ball of yarn' happen when you are talking to friends or family in a relaxed setting, or does it only seem to occur when you are under pressure at work?
turns.patient_response:
Well, that’s exactly it, doctor, that’s actually the main reason I finally decided I needed to come in and see somebody about this. I originally thought it was just the stress of the retail environment, you know? Because it definitely happens at the store. I'll be standing there trying to explain the inventory numbers for the new quarter, or maybe I’m just trying to lay out the weekend schedule for the floor staff—which is always a headache anyway because nobody ever wants to work the Sunday morning opening shift—and the words just get entirely derailed. 

But then I realized it’s not just work. It’s happening everywhere, even when I'm completely relaxed. I’ll start out trying to talk about something simple, and then my words start jumping all over the place without my permission. I’ll go from talking about the delivery trucks we're expecting, and then that makes me say something about Thursdays, because Thursday is when the big freight truck comes in, but then suddenly I'm talking about the church grill—we have this massive, heavy-duty charcoal grill we use for the parish summer fundraisers, I've been manning it for a decade—and then before I can even catch myself, I'm going on about my boss’s tone of voice from a conference call he ran three weeks ago. 

It just leaps from one thing to the next. Trucks to Thursdays to the church grill to my boss's tone, all strung together in the same breath like it's supposed to make perfect sense. And whether it's my employees by the stockroom doors or my own family at a Sunday barbecue, they all do the exact same thing. They just stop, and they stare at me, and they get this deeply confused look on their faces... people just look at me like they absolutely can’t follow what I’m saying. It’s like they're trying to read a map that's been put through a paper shredder. So, no, it's definitely not just when I'm under pressure at the store. It's happening when I'm just trying to have a normal, relaxed conversation, too, and it's making it nearly impossible to just sit down and talk to people without feeling like I'm speaking a foreign language.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient describes their speech derailing and jumping between unrelated topics (trucks, Thursdays, church grill, boss's tone) to the point where others cannot follow what they are saying, confirming disorganized thinking and speech.

turns.doctor_question: When you try to write down your thoughts or tasks in your planner, do you find that your writing also becomes jumbled and disorganized, or is it only your spoken words that seem to get tangled?
turns.patient_response:
Writing it down? Well, it’s funny you ask that, because I actually carry a planner with me everywhere. It's a little black leather-bound one—my daughter got it for me for Father's Day a couple of years back, actually—and I have a very specific system for it. I always write in blue ink, never black, because black looks too much like printed text and it blends in, you know? And if I sit down in my office, close the door, and just focus on the paper... I can usually get the tasks down. I can write out the inventory numbers. I can write out the weekend schedule. The ink on the page usually makes sense. 

But the second I have to actually *talk* about what I just wrote... well, that’s exactly what I was just telling you about. That’s the whole reason I came in here today. I'll have that planner right there in my hand, open to the right page, and I'll try to explain those inventory numbers or that weekend schedule to the floor staff, and instead of just saying what I wrote, my mouth just takes off on its own. 

Like I was just saying, it doesn't matter if it's written down right in front of me, my words still start jumping from the delivery trucks, to Thursdays, to that heavy church grill, all the way to my boss’s tone of voice on a conference call. It just completely detaches from what's on the paper. I could have it bullet-pointed perfectly, color-coded even, but when I try to speak it out loud, the words just scatter everywhere. And then I'm left standing there holding my nice leather planner while people just look at me like they absolutely can’t follow a single thing I’m saying. So, I suppose the writing itself is mostly okay, as long as I have quiet time to do it, but it doesn't do me any good once I actually have to open my mouth. The talking is where all the wires get crossed.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient confirms that their speech is highly disorganized, jumping between unrelated topics like trucks, Thursdays, and a church grill, leaving others unable to follow what they are saying.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient denies difficulty organizing tasks, explaining that they use a highly specific, bullet-pointed, and color-coded system in their planner to successfully organize their tasks and schedules.

turns.doctor_question: If I were to ask you to repeat the phrase 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' back to me right now, would you be able to do that clearly, or would the words get jumbled in the same way?
turns.patient_response:
Well, "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"—I mean, I could probably say that right now without a hitch. Let's see... "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog." See? Clear as day. But, doctor, with all due respect, that’s just a memorized trick from middle school typing class. I remember typing that exact sentence over and over on an old Smith Corona manual typewriter back in the late seventies, trying to get my words-per-minute up. 

Repeating a memorized line like a parrot isn't where the wires get crossed for me. It's when I have to actually put my own thoughts together and construct a conversation that matters. Like I’ve been trying to tell you—and really, I can't stress enough that this is the entire reason I'm sitting in this chair today—the problem isn't reciting a nursery rhyme. It's when I have to explain the actual inventory numbers for the store, or when I'm trying to lay out that weekend schedule for the staff. 

I know I keep bringing up those same examples, but it's just the absolute perfect illustration of how bad this has gotten. I'll start out talking about the schedule, and then, just like I was explaining a minute ago, my words start jumping entirely on their own. They jump from the schedule to the delivery trucks, to Thursdays, to that heavy charcoal church grill, all the way to the exact tone of voice my regional manager used on a call three weeks ago. It's a total cascade. And I can see it happening in real-time because the people I'm talking to—they just freeze. They look at me like they absolutely cannot follow what I’m saying. They get this blank, concerned stare like I've suddenly started speaking Greek. 

So, sure, the fox and the dog are perfectly fine. My mouth can handle that. But if you ask me to explain my actual day to you, or manage my team, that's when the train comes completely off the tracks.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient explicitly describes their words jumping from topic to topic (schedule, trucks, Thursdays, church grill, manager's tone) and people being unable to follow what they are saying, which is a clear description of disorganized thinking and speech (derailment/loose associations).

turns.doctor_question: When your speech becomes jumbled like that, do you find that your tongue or lips feel like they are physically struggling to move correctly, or does it feel like your brain is simply choosing the wrong words or ideas to express?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, it's nothing physical like that. My tongue and my lips, they work perfectly fine. I mean, I’ve been in retail management for decades, I spend eight, ten hours a day on my feet just talking to people, so the physical act of speaking is practically muscle memory at this point. I never feel like I'm slurring or physically tripping over my teeth, nothing like that. It’s definitely the other thing you said—it’s the ideas. It's like my brain is just pulling files from completely different cabinets and throwing them all on the desk at the exact same time. 

Like I keep telling you—and I know I must sound like a broken record by now, going on and on about the same exact situations, but I really just want you to understand because this is exactly why I finally came in here to see you—when I try to explain those inventory numbers or that weekend schedule, my mouth is doing its job perfectly. But my brain just takes the steering wheel and starts jumping. It jumps right from the schedule to those delivery trucks, and then to Thursdays, and then to that heavy church grill, and then right into my boss’s tone of voice. 

It’s all happening up here, in the thoughts. My mouth just blindly follows along and says whatever my brain decides to spit out, no matter how little sense it makes. And that’s exactly why people look at me like they absolutely can’t follow what I’m saying. They hear the words clearly, my enunciation is fine, but the ideas are just... they're from four different conversations mashed into one. So, no, physically speaking I'm fine, it's just the thoughts themselves that are running completely wild and dragging my mouth along for the ride.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient describes their speech and ideas jumping illogically between unrelated topics (trucks, Thursdays, church grill, boss's tone) making it impossible for others to follow, which indicates disorganized thinking and speech (derailment/loose associations).
symptom_reasoning.S038: The patient describes their thoughts as 'running completely wild' and their brain 'pulling files from completely different cabinets and throwing them all on the desk at the exact same time,' indicating racing thoughts or flight of ideas.

turns.doctor_question: When your thoughts start jumping around like that, do you ever feel like you are seeing, hearing, or sensing things that other people in the room don't seem to notice?
turns.patient_response:
Seeing or hearing things? No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I know exactly why you might ask that, because when I get going and my words are scattering all over the place, I'm sure it looks to the people around me like I'm completely detached from reality, maybe talking to a ghost or hearing voices or something. I'm sure that's exactly what they're thinking when they give me that blank stare. But no, my eyes and ears work just as well as they ever did. 

If I'm standing in the back room with my assistant manager—let's say it's Dave, he's a good kid, been with us about three years now, studying business at the community college—if I'm standing there with Dave, I'm looking at the exact same cardboard boxes he is. I'm hearing the exact same terrible soft-rock station that corporate mandates we play on the overhead speakers. I don't see anything that isn't there, and I don't hear anything that isn't actually happening. 

It's really just... it's all internal. It's just the thoughts themselves. Like I've been trying to explain, and I really want to make sure we keep focusing on this because this is the absolute root of the whole problem... when I'm looking right at Dave, seeing him perfectly clearly, my brain just decides to pull up those delivery trucks, and then Thursdays, and then that heavy church grill, and my boss’s tone of voice. I'm not *hearing* my boss's voice in the room with me, you understand? I'm just suddenly *talking* about it when I'm supposed to be talking about the weekend schedule. 

So no, I'm not sensing anything secret or invisible. My senses are fine. It's just my brain throwing all those different files onto the desk at once, and my mouth just running away with them while I'm standing there looking at the exact same normal stockroom as everybody else.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient describes their words "scattering all over the place" and suddenly talking about unrelated topics instead of the task at hand, indicating disorganized speech and derailment.
symptom_reasoning.S038: The patient describes their brain "throwing all those different files onto the desk at once," reflecting the subjective experience of racing thoughts or flight of ideas.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies seeing or hearing things that aren't there, confirming they do not experience hallucinations.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any changes in your personality, such as becoming more impulsive, having less of a filter in what you say to others, or acting differently than you typically would?
turns.patient_response:
Impulsive... no, I wouldn't say impulsive. I've never been a hothead, and I'm certainly not losing my filter and cursing out the cashiers or anything like that. I've always been a planner, you know? You don't survive in retail management for decades by flying by the seat of your pants. But acting differently? Yes. Absolutely, yes. And it's... well, it's incredibly frustrating, and honestly a bit embarrassing, because I know it's not how I usually run my shift. 

I catch myself doing these things on the sales floor that just make no sense. Like, sometimes I'll be out there, and I'll just start pacing. I'll pace the exact same aisle, back and forth, back and forth. Usually it's over by the front end, the impulse buy section, and I'll just be straightening the same row of batteries over and over again. I'm talking about taking the double-A packs, making sure they're perfectly flush on the little metal peg, then moving to the triple-As, and then going right back to the double-As and doing it all over again. I've been doing this job long enough to know when an endcap is faced properly and looks fine, but I just get stuck doing it repeatedly. 

Or—and this ties right back into that weekend schedule I keep bringing up, because it really is the perfect example of how this is affecting my job—I'll just be standing there right in the middle of the main action alley with the schedule clipboard in my hand. Just standing completely still. And the associates, they'll be gathered around, waiting for me to tell them what to do. They need direction, they need to know who is covering the registers for lunch breaks or who is pulling stock from the back, and I'm just planted there staring at the clipboard like it's a paperweight. 

So it's not that I'm suddenly acting wild or saying inappropriate things, it's just... I get stuck in these weird, pointless physical loops, or I just freeze up entirely when I'm supposed to be actively managing the floor. So yes, my behavior out there has definitely changed, and it's completely throwing off the rhythm of the whole team.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes getting stuck in pointless physical loops like pacing and repeatedly straightening batteries, as well as freezing up and standing completely still (stupor/posturing).
symptom_reasoning.S041: The patient explicitly denies becoming impulsive or acting wildly.
symptom_reasoning.S077: The patient denies being a 'hothead' or losing their filter to curse out cashiers, ruling out verbal aggression and impulsive anger.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any new physical symptoms like tremors, twitching, or any unusual stiffness in your arms or legs?
turns.patient_response:
Tremors? Twitching? No, no, nothing like that. Like I was saying a few minutes ago when you asked about my mouth and my tongue, physically, my body is doing exactly what it's supposed to do. I mean, I'm fifty-nine years old, so I'm not going to sit here and tell you my knees don't ache a little bit after an eight or ten-hour shift on those hard concrete floors. You work retail for decades like I have, you're going to get some normal wear and tear on the joints. But unusual stiffness? Or shaking? Absolutely not. My hands are perfectly steady. 

When I'm holding that clipboard with the weekend schedule—and I know I keep coming back to the clipboard, but it really is the clearest way I can think of to explain what's happening to me out there—when I'm standing there frozen in the main action alley, it's not because my arms are physically stiff. It's not like my muscles are locking up or paralyzed or anything like that. I could physically drop the clipboard, or wave my arms, or walk away, if my brain would just send the proper signal to do it. The muscles themselves are fine. And there's no twitching, no shaking, no weird stiffness in my legs when I'm doing that pacing by the impulse buy section either. My stride is perfectly normal when I'm walking back and forth by those batteries. 

It's just the mental loop I get stuck in, like I was telling you. So, as far as my actual body goes... my arms, my legs, my hands... they're all perfectly fine. It's just the management upstairs that's completely dropping the ball, if you catch my drift. The physical equipment is in perfect working order, so I haven't noticed any shakes or stiffness at all.

symptom_reasoning.S061: The patient explicitly denies experiencing any unusual muscle stiffness, stating their muscles are fine and not locking up.

turns.doctor_question: When you find yourself standing still in the aisle with your clipboard, if someone were to gently try to move your arm or change your position, would you feel physically resistant, or would your body stay exactly where they placed it?
turns.patient_response:
If someone tried to move my arm? Well... honestly, I couldn't tell you for sure because nobody has actually ever tried to do that. The associates, you know, they respect the hierarchy. They see the supervisor badge, they aren't going to just walk up and start manhandling me, even if I am acting a bit strange. 

Like I was just saying a minute ago, when I'm just standing there with the schedule clipboard in my hand—and they're all gathered around waiting for me to tell them what to do, waiting to hear who is covering the front registers or who is pulling the pallets from the back—they just sort of look at each other. They don't touch me. But if they *did*? No, I wouldn't feel physically resistant. I wouldn't fight them on it. And I definitely wouldn't just leave my arm hovering in mid-air wherever they posed it, like some kind of department store mannequin. 

Like I said, the muscles themselves are perfectly fine. It’s more just... well, it goes right back to what I was telling you about my behavior out there. Sometimes on the sales floor I'll just catch myself pacing that exact same aisle, or straightening that same row of batteries over and over, or just standing there completely still with that clipboard while everyone waits on me. It’s not that my body is locked up or stiff. It's just that the command center up top has stopped issuing new orders, so I just keep doing the same useless repetitive thing, or doing nothing at all. 

If Dave or one of the cashiers actually reached out and grabbed my arm or tried to turn me around, I'm sure it would just startle me and I'd pull my arm right back down normally. I'm sure it would snap me right out of it. But they don't. They just wait. Because it's awkward for them, isn't it? Approaching your boss when he's just staring into space. So I just stand there, or I pace, until the gears finally catch again and I realize what I'm doing.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient confirms experiencing repetitive, purposeless behaviors (pacing, straightening batteries over and over) and periods of standing completely still (stupor or posturing), which are forms of disorganized or abnormal motor behavior, despite denying specific catatonic features like waxy flexibility.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any changes in your ability to control your bladder or bowels, such as sudden urgency or accidents, since this began?
turns.patient_response:
Bladder or bowels? Oh, goodness, no. No, nothing like that at all. Like I was just saying about my muscles and my joints and everything else, the physical machinery of my body is running just fine. 

I mean, think about it—if I had sudden urgency or, heaven forbid, an accident, working in retail management would be an absolute nightmare. The restrooms in our store, the employee ones anyway, they’re all the way in the back corner past the receiving bays, right next to the breakroom. If I'm up at the front end, pacing by that impulse buy section like I was telling you about, straightening those double-A batteries over and over... if I suddenly had to go, it's a good two or three-minute walk just to get back there. And that's if you don't get stopped by a customer asking where the furnace filters are, or an associate needing a manager override on register four. You just can't run to the bathroom whenever you feel like it in my line of work, you have to wait for proper floor coverage. 

So, no, I have perfect control. I've always been very regular. I usually just go once before my shift starts, maybe once during my lunch break, and I'm good for the rest of the day. Even when I get stuck standing there in the main action alley with that weekend schedule clipboard, just completely frozen while Dave and the cashiers are waiting on me to tell them who is pulling stock from the back... even then, it's never because I'm having some sort of bathroom emergency. It's strictly a mental roadblock. I haven't soiled myself or had to rush off the floor suddenly. 

Thank God for that, honestly, because like I said, it’s already embarrassing enough just standing there staring into space while my team looks at me. If I had an accident on top of it in front of everyone? I'd have to hand in my store keys right then and there, I could never show my face again. So, no, absolutely no changes in that department. Everything down there is working exactly the way it always has.

symptom_reasoning.S031: The patient describes experiencing a 'mental roadblock' and being 'completely frozen' and 'staring into space' when trying to make a decision about assigning tasks to staff, indicating indecisiveness and diminished thinking.

turns.doctor_question: When you are having these moments where your thoughts feel jumbled or you feel stuck, do you ever find yourself becoming convinced that people are talking about you behind your back, or that your colleagues are intentionally trying to sabotage your work?
turns.patient_response:
Talking behind my back? Sabotage? Oh, heavens, no. No, no, no, nothing like that. 

I mean... look, retail is retail, right? Any time you have an employee breakroom, you're going to have a little bit of gossip. That’s just human nature. You get a bunch of twenty-somethings working for near minimum wage, they're going to complain about management, they're going to complain about their hours, they're going to complain about the customers. That's just the reality of the business, and after doing this for as long as I have, you develop a pretty thick skin about the normal day-to-day chatter. 

But as far as them actually plotting against me? Or intentionally trying to sabotage my work? Not at all. I don't believe that for a second. Take Dave, for instance, the cashier I was mentioning earlier. Dave is a good kid. He’s been on the front end for almost two years now, and he’s just trying to pay his way through community college. He doesn't care enough about the corporate ladder to try and sabotage a fifty-nine-year-old floor supervisor. Honestly, none of them do. They just want to punch in, do their eight hours, and punch out. 

When I'm having those moments—when I'm just standing there in the main action alley, completely stuck, staring at that weekend schedule on my clipboard like it's written in ancient Greek—they aren't whispering about how to ruin my career. They aren't scheming. They're just... waiting. They're probably just thinking, "Come on, old man, just tell me if I'm on register four or if I'm pulling pallets from receiving so I can get this shift over with." 

It's not malicious. If anything, they're probably just annoyed because my delay means their fifteen-minute break gets pushed back. So, no, I don't have any grand theories about them being out to get me or talking about me behind my back. The only person sabotaging my work right now is me, honestly, with this... this mental roadblock, or whatever it is that keeps happening. It's all on my end. The associates are just innocent bystanders caught in the crossfire of my brain stalling out while I'm supposed to be delegating tasks. So I definitely don't blame them, and I certainly don't think they're out to get me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies believing that his colleagues are plotting against him or intentionally trying to sabotage his work.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever find yourself feeling that there is a special, hidden meaning behind the way your coworkers arrange the items on the shelves, or that the way they place products is a secret message directed specifically at you?
turns.patient_response:
Hidden meaning? Secret messages in the... in the products? Oh, no. No, definitely not. 

You see, in retail—especially at our level, with the corporate structure we have—there is absolutely no room for creativity on the shelves to begin with. It’s all dictated by the planograms. I don't know if you're familiar with how that works, but a planogram is basically this highly detailed schematic sent down from corporate. We get them every quarter, sometimes every month for the seasonal aisles or the promotional endcaps, and they tell us exactly where every single SKU is supposed to go, down to the exact inch. 

So if Dave is stocking the soup aisle, or if one of the newer associates is setting up a display of paper towels, they aren't arranging them to send me some kind of cryptic message. They're just following the binder. It’s supposed to be two facings of chicken noodle, three facings of tomato, all the labels facing out, pulled flush to the front edge of the shelf—what we call "zoning" or "facing" the store. 

I mean, if I walk down an aisle and see that someone put the generic store-brand cereal where the name-brand is supposed to go, I don't look at that and think it's a secret code directed at me. I just think... well, I just think it's laziness, or that they weren't paying attention to the barcodes on the shelf tags, and now I'm going to have to go over there and have them fix it. Which, honestly, is part of why I get so frustrated when I have those moments where I just freeze up with my clipboard. Because I know the shelves need to be zoned, I know the district manager might be doing a walkthrough on Tuesday, and instead of directing my team to fix the shelves, I just... I just stand there. 

But no, I don't look at a display of canned goods or the battery rack I keep pacing past and think it means something special. A battery is just a battery. A crooked box of cereal is just a crooked box of cereal. There's no secret code going on. The associates are just trying to get the freight off the pallets and onto the floor before the morning rush hits, that's all there is to it. If they actually wanted to send me a message, they’d just write it on a sticky note and leave it on the desk in the back office, you know? So, no, nothing like that at all. Just the standard corporate layouts.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies believing that there are hidden meanings or secret messages directed at them in the way products are arranged, attributing the arrangements to corporate planograms instead.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever feel as though your own thoughts are being broadcast out loud so that others can hear them, or that someone or something is inserting thoughts into your mind that do not belong to you?
turns.patient_response:
Broadcast out loud? Like over the store intercom? Oh, goodness, no. Could you imagine? I mean, really, could you imagine the absolute chaos if the things I was thinking were just playing out loud for everyone to hear? 

If that were happening, if Dave and the rest of the front-end team could actually hear what I was thinking when I'm staring at that weekend schedule, they'd probably just hear me doing mental math, trying to figure out how to cover lunches when two cashiers call out sick on a busy Saturday afternoon. That's all that's really up there most of the time. Just payroll budgets and break schedules and wondering if receiving ever finished unloading the seasonal truck. But no, nobody can hear any of that. My thoughts stay right here in my own head, completely private. Honestly, sometimes I almost wish people could hear them, because then when I get stuck standing there in the main action alley, completely frozen up like I was telling you, at least they would know I'm actually trying to figure out the floor coverage instead of just staring into space like a department store mannequin. 

And as for someone putting thoughts into my head? Or inserting things that don't belong to me? No, no, definitely not. My thoughts are one hundred percent my own. I have a Bachelor's degree in business administration, I've been managing people and store operations for decades, I certainly don't need anyone or anything else putting thoughts into my head to do my job. The problem I'm having isn't that there are foreign thoughts in there, or that someone is messing with my mind from the outside. The problem is just that sometimes the thoughts I do have just... stop. Or they get jammed up, you know, like a broken receipt printer when the paper rolls back on itself. 

It's just my own brain stalling out on me. Nobody is beaming anything into my mind, and I'm certainly not broadcasting anything out to the associates or the customers. It's just me, my clipboard, and my own frustrating inability to just spit out the directions to my team when I need to. So, no, nothing like broadcasting or inserted thoughts. Just my own normal, everyday work thoughts, even if they do get stuck in traffic up there sometimes.
